title: Coleman Hawkins and the effect of Stampede
summary: The Hawkins solo on Fletcher Henderson's Stampede eclipsed all other tenor players for Tate's generation.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: Well, tell me about "Stampede." What was the --

Well, it was like -- I don't know, he was swinging so on "Stampede" and it was a terrific arrangement of Fletcher's in the first place. Everything was right there. And I'll never forget, it was in A flat and they played clarinets and it was just a hell of an arrangement, you know, absolutely fantastic arrangement and it was just made for him and he just upset everybody when he made it. He made, you
know, such a fantastic solo. I guess you could compare it to like when Lester made "Lester Leaps In," you know, one of those things, you know.
Had you been aware of Hawkins before?

Yeah. Yeah, I knew he was with Fletcher and I had listened to him, but I wasn't really -- he wasn't my idol -- Prince is like -- as much as Prince was, you know, until, of course, after that, I loved him, you know, I really did love him. And then everybody was like -- he gained the recognition as being the world's greatest saxophone player, you know, tenor player, because he really did really introduce the instrument. There's no stuff about that, you know, like even when Mamie Smith, when he was playing with Mamie Smith before Fletcher Henderson, he was playing the tenor then and he was popular, because the horn was the alto and the C melody.
